sentences.text: The type species P. latipinnis was a medium-sized plesiosaur with a short neck, measuring between 4.7 and 5.4 meters in length and weighing over 1 metric ton.
Like other plesiosaurs, Polycotylus was a large marine reptile with a short tail, large flippers, and a broad body. It had an elongated head reaching lengths of up to 5 meters.
Distinctive features include long pelvic ischia, thick striated teeth, a narrow pterygoid bone, and a low sagittal crest on the skull.
Polycotylus is distinguished from other well-known plesiosaurs like Plesiosaurus and Elasmosaurus by having a short neck.
Polycotylus and other polycotylids superficially resemble pliosaurs like Liopleurodon and Peloneustes due to their short necks, large heads, and body proportions that differ from other plesiosaurs.
A fossil of an adult Polycotylus containing a large fetus provides evidence that the animal gave live birth, an unusual trait for reptiles.
The fetus found inside the adult Polycotylus fossil was approximately 1.5 meters long, representing about 32 percent of the mother's length.
F. Robin O'Keefe, one of the describers of the specimen, suggests that the social lives of plesiosaurs were more similar to those of modern dolphins than to other reptiles.
Edward Drinker Cope originally described Polycotylus based on fossils from the Niobrara Formation in Kansas in 1869.
The genus Polycotylus was named by Cope in 1869.
A nearly complete skeleton of Polycotylus found in Alabama in 1949 was not formally described until 2002.
A more complete skeleton of Polycotylus found in Kansas was described in 1906.
The fossil LACM 129639 was found in Kansas in the 1980s and stored at the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History until it was described in 2011.
Fossil evidence suggests that Polycotylus was viviparous, giving birth to live young rather than laying eggs.
This fossil suggests that Polycotylus was viviparous, giving birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
LACM 129639 was the first direct evidence of viviparity in plesiosaurs.
Analysis of Polycotylus fetuses indicates that they sacrificed bone strength in the womb to achieve accelerated growth rates.
Based on knowledge of fetal development in their relatives the nothosaurs, gestation was probably completed at two-thirds.
Researchers believe the mother Polycotylus provided parental care to its single large offspring to ensure its survival.
Because it gave birth to a single large offspring, the mother Polycotylus probably provided some form of care to ensure its survival.
The lives of Polycotylus and other plesiosaurs followed a K-selection strategy, meaning few offspring were born per individual but each new offspring was cared for until maturity.
The genus Polycotylus includes the type species P. latipinnis and the species P. sopozkoi.
The genus Polycotylus includes several species such as P. latipinnis, P. ichthyospondylus, and P. tenius, along with several nomina dubia.
Due to its short neck, Polycotylus was historically classified as a pliosaur within the superfamily Pliosauroidea, though it is closely related to true plesiosaurs.
In 1997, phylogenetic analyses reassigned Polycotylus as a close relative of long-necked elasmosaurids.
In 1997, polycotylids were reassigned as close relatives of long-necked elasmosaurids.
In a 2001 study, Polycotylus was classified as a derived cryptocleidoid plesiosaur closely related to Jurassic plesiosaurs like Cryptocleidus.
Polycotylus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Campanian stages, between 152.21 and 72.2 million years ago.
Polycotylus lived in the Western Interior Seaway of North America near the end of the Cretaceous period.
Polycotylus lived in the seas of North America, Russia, and Australia during the late Cretaceous.
It is debated whether viviparity was the most common reproductive strategy in plesiosaurs due to the difficulty of laying eggs on land.
